E ON THE BEST CURVATURE SPLITTING PROBLEM (see Section 4)

In Section 4 we examined how to achieve the optimal splitting for a given objective F = fı - f2 by subtracting the same curvature term 1'!' in both functions. We concluded that if 41 ≤ 2, the best splitting is achieved by shifting the lower curvature of fı to 0, i.e., make it convex. Conversely, when p1 > M2, the best splitting is achieved for some f2 weakly convex, with lower curvature 42 - 1 < 0. Within this section, we provide additional numerical experiments. In Figure 10 we provide an example with fixed curvature bounds of a nonconvex-nonconcave objective function F, namely UF = -0.5 and LF = 1.5, and illustrate all possible regimes after one iteration. Note that uF = 41 - L2 and LF = L1 - 42; further on, we examine the regimes based on the ranges of L2 and 42. The condition 41 ≥ 0 implies that L2 = H1 - UF ≥ -UF, while the condition 41 + H2 > 0 that 42 > -41 = L2 + MF. The contour lines represent the values of the denominators pi, with i = 1,2,3, 4. The red points mark the initial curvature values of L2 and M2, whereas the green dots indicate the points with the largest possible pi obtained through the optimal choice of 1. Since these shifts are linear in 1, the dashed lines connecting the dots have a slope of one. For example, in the case where L2 = 1 and 42 = 0.75, we have 41 < 42 and the best splitting is obtained by shifting to the lowest possible value of L2, corresponding to 41 = 0. In all other examples, N1 > H2 and the optimal splittings are found within regime p3, where 42 < 0
